title: Practice Set DM1 — Filtering: What Stays, What Goes
description: Recognition track: read filter expressions and predict which rows survive. Empty strings vs nulls, three filter idioms compared. Companion to the Foundations Filtering chapter.

datasets.description: NordGrid meter readings (10–20 rows depending on exercise). Most exercises use a smaller inline sample shown in the Evidence panel; this file is the schema-level reference.
Substations reference (6 rows). Used in cleaning + type-casting exercises.

tasks.title: The Empty String Is Not A Null

description.context: Pandas treats two kinds of 'missing' very differently. A null is the special value NaN (or pd.NA) — Pandas marks the cell as 'no data here'. An empty string '' is a real string of length zero — Pandas treats it as a present value, just one with no characters. The method `notna()` only returns False for the null kind; it returns True for the empty string. The comparison `!= ''` only returns False for the empty string; for nulls, comparison-with-null returns null which Pandas treats as falsy in a boolean mask. So the two filters drop overlapping but DIFFERENT sets of rows. CSV readers commonly produce both kinds in the same column when upstream sources are inconsistent.
description.task: How many rows does each filter keep?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: A 10-row sample of NordGrid meter readings. Two rows have an empty string in `region`, two rows have a true null, and six rows have a regular region value.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Two candidate filters. Both are intended to 'keep only rows with a region'.
result_a = df[df['region'].notna()]
result_b = df[df['region'] != '']

fields.label: How many rows does each filter keep?
options: result_a keeps 8 rows, result_b keeps 8 rows — notna() and != '' are interchangeable ways to ask 'is there a value here', so both filters drop the same four rows (two empties + two nulls).

result_a keeps 8 rows, result_b keeps 6 rows — notna() drops only true nulls, so the two empty-string rows survive in result_a; != '' drops the empty strings (and the nulls compare as falsy), giving 6 rows in result_b.
result_a keeps 6 rows, result_b keeps 8 rows — != '' is the looser check because it only inspects the empty-string condition; notna() is the stricter filter and drops both nulls and empties.
result_a keeps 6 rows, result_b keeps 6 rows — Pandas treats '' and null as the same missing-value sentinel, so notna() and != '' end up dropping the same union of rows.
fields.correctAnswer: result_a keeps 8 rows, result_b keeps 6 rows — notna() drops only true nulls, so the two empty-string rows survive in result_a; != '' drops the empty strings (and the nulls compare as falsy), giving 6 rows in result_b.
fields.rationale: The two filters target different things. notna() returns True for any value that is not a true null — and the empty string '' is not a null, it is a real string of length zero. So the two empty-string rows (M-003, M-007) pass notna() and stay in result_a (8 rows). The != '' check returns False for those empty-string rows and null-when-compared-to-null for the nulls (also falsy), so result_b drops all four (6 rows). The most common Junior confusion is treating '' and null as the same kind of 'missing'; Pandas treats them as two distinct categories.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats notna() and != '' as the same operation. The exact misconception this exercise targets — '' is not a null in Pandas.

Option C: Reverses which filter is stricter. != '' is the stricter one because it drops both empties and nulls; notna() drops only nulls.

Option D: Conflates '' with null as a single 'missing' sentinel. Pandas keeps them distinct categories and the two methods disagree on which to treat as missing.

tasks.title: Three Filter Idioms, Three Different Behaviors

description.context: Pandas offers three common ways to subset a DataFrame and Junior engineers often assume they are interchangeable. Boolean mask indexing (`df[df['col'] > x]`) builds a True/False array and keeps the True rows. The `.query()` method takes a STRING expression that Pandas parses internally; it is row-filtering. The `.filter()` method has a misleading name — it does NOT filter rows by a predicate. It selects COLUMNS by name (or rows by INDEX label, but never by a value condition). Knowing what each idiom actually does matters because they can produce the same row count on a sample dataset for the wrong reason.
description.task: On the 10-row test dataset all three idioms produce 6 rows. Which statement about them is correct?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 10-row sample of NordGrid meter readings used by all three idioms below.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Three idioms, all targeting 'keep rows where daily_kw > 1000'.

# Idiom A — boolean mask indexing
result_a = df[df['daily_kw'] > 1000]

# Idiom B — the query() method with a string expression
result_b = df.query('daily_kw > 1000')

# Idiom C — the filter() method (often misused on rows; it actually filters columns)
result_c = df.filter(items=['daily_kw']).loc[df['daily_kw'] > 1000]

fields.label: On the 10-row test dataset all three idioms produce 6 rows. Which statement about them is correct?
options: All three idioms route through the same internal Pandas filter path and the choice between them is just style — boolean masking, query(), and filter() are documented as aliases for the same row-predicate operation.

Idiom B is the differentiator: query() fails on column names with spaces or hyphens because its string parser is restricted, while idioms A and C work on any column name and on this test dataset they all happen to produce 6 rows.

Idiom A returns a view, idiom B returns a copy, and idiom C returns a copy-of-a-subset — the row counts match by coincidence, but only A may trigger SettingWithCopyWarning, so A is the one to avoid in production.

Idiom C does not actually filter rows — DataFrame.filter() selects COLUMNS (here just daily_kw via items=[...]); the row predicate is done by the .loc[...] that follows. Same row count by coincidence, very different operation.
fields.correctAnswer: Idiom C does not actually filter rows — DataFrame.filter() selects COLUMNS (here just daily_kw via items=[...]); the row predicate is done by the .loc[...] that follows. Same row count by coincidence, very different operation.
fields.rationale: DataFrame.filter() is named misleadingly. It does not filter rows by predicate — it selects columns (or rows by index LABEL). The items=['daily_kw'] argument keeps only the daily_kw column. The actual row predicate in idiom C is the .loc[df['daily_kw'] > 1000] that follows. The 6-row match on this dataset is coincidental — change the test data and idiom C drops most of the columns the team expected to keep. The most common Junior confusion is reading 'filter' and assuming row predicate; in Pandas, filter() is a column-selection method.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats all three as the same operation. query() has its own parser; filter() does something entirely different — they are not aliases.

Option B: Identifies a real query() quirk but it is not what makes idiom C different on this dataset.

Option C: Mixes a real view-vs-copy concern with wrong attribution; the load-bearing fact is that filter() is not row-filtering at all.
